subject: Proposal: hybrid on‑prem node segmentation and archival PV lifecycle
messages:
From: Andrew Li <andrew@peregrinedatalabs.com>
To: irene_choi@redwood.inference.com
Cc: Ops Team <ops@peregrinedatalabs.com>
Date: Wed, 10 Feb 2027 10:15:00 -0800
Subject: Private cluster: hybrid segmentation + long‑term archive questions

Hi Irene,

Thanks again for the walkthrough this morning. We discussed a hybrid approach for our on‑prem clusters where latency‑sensitive inference workloads live on a tiny fast nodeclass while archival and periodic batch retraining jobs run on dense, high‑capacity nodes. Before we commit to the Dedicated contract, the infra team needs clarity on a few items so we can finalize rack/cabling and procurement: 

1) Proposal for node segmentation — how to size the fast inference nodepool vs archival nodepool for the first 12 months (we expect ~1.2M inference tokens / day, and ~200 TB of model weights + snapshots that grow ~30% q/q).
2) PVC lifecycle — best practice for binding / eviction to ensure hot caches remain local while older snapshots are moved to tape/nearline.
3) Egress & CDN interplay — we serve model outputs to global users via a CDN; how should we handle egress NAT and signed URL generation from the on‑prem control plane?
4) Compliance traceability — we need a simple mapping of audit logs (token-level metadata) to our internal dataset IDs for SOC readiness.

Can you send a short runbook or decision matrix we can hand to procurement and our data security folks? Prefer a one‑pager plus sample PV lifecycle matrix if possible.

Cheers,
Andrew
Andrew Li
CTO, Peregrine Data Labs

Subject: Re: Private cluster: hybrid segmentation + long‑term archive questions

Andrew —

Appreciate the clear list. I put together a short plan below and attached a draft runbook + a PV lifecycle matrix (high level) for your procurement/security teams. Key recommendations up front: keep inference nodepool small and fast with KV cache affinity, and carve archival storage as a separate nodeclass with lifecycle hooks to offload to nearline on a retention cadence.

1) Node segmentation (first 12 months):
- Inference nodepool: 4 x G4‑equivalent nodes (or 8 x smaller GPUs) as a starting point with a target p95 latency SLO of 150ms for your workload profile. Autoscale threshold: 65% GPU util sustained over 5m.
- Archive nodepool: 6 x high‑density CPU+NVMe servers, dedicated PVs for snapshots; treat as burstable batch workers rather than low‑latency frontends.
- Buffer pool: 2 small nodes reserved for cache warming and prefetch (reduces cold start penalties during rollouts).

Sizing rationale: based on your 1.2M tokens/day and typical Redwood token throughput, the above should give steady capacity with headroom for a 2x burst. We’ll provide per‑token cost estimates in a follow up.

2) PVC lifecycle (recommended pattern):
- Use two storage classes: fast‑ssd (ReadWriteOnce, local NVMe where possible) for model KV caches and hot weights; bulk‑archive (ReadWriteMany, replicated object backing) mounted on archival nodepool.
- Implement a lifecycle controller (we provide an example in the attached matrix): tags = {dataset_id, snapshot_ts, retention_days}. Controller actions:
  * Day 0–30: keep snapshot pinned to fast‑ssd for retraining and rollbacks.
  * Day 31–90: move snapshot to bulk‑archive (nearline) and keep lightweight index on fast‑ssd.
  * >90 days: mark eligible for tape/nearline export (S3 Glacier or on‑prem tape job).
- Eviction policy: never evict KV cache entries tied to active inference pods; use graceful eviction and prefetch to buffer pool if we need to drain nodes.

3) Egress & CDN:
- Push signed URLs from Redwood control plane; egress NAT should terminate at a small edge gateway in your VPC (we recommend one per site) that handles rate limiting and rewritten headers for CDN origin pulls.
- If you need per‑token telemetry, proxy signed requests through the control plane to emit minimal metadata (request id, user id hash, dataset_id) to your audit pipeline. Avoid sending raw payloads to external CDNs for compliance reasons.

4) Compliance traceability:
- We can augment the request metadata with a 1:1 mapping to your dataset IDs using an immutable header X‑RDW‑Dataset that the control plane records in our audit logs. Audit logs include timestamptz, route, model_id, runtime_variant, dataset_id. We will provide a sample mapping CSV in the runbook.

Next steps / asks from you:
- Confirm whether you prefer local NVMe for fast‑ssd or a cloud‑backed NVMe appliance (we included both options in the runbook).
- Share retention policy for snapshots (we assumed 90 days in matrix).
- Any procurement constraints (rack U, preferred OEMs, procurement lead) so we can align BOM.

I’ve attached:
- peregrine-runbook-draft.pdf (one‑pager + sample PV lifecycle table)
- pv-lifecycle-matrix.xlsx (spreadsheet with triggers and controller actions)

If helpful, Laura can scope a tighter capacity model tomorrow.

—Irene
Irene Choi
Head of Product — Private Deployments
Redwood Inference

Andrew — quick follow up on sizing details from an ops/IO perspective: 

- Inference nodepool: assume 8 vCPU + 64GB RAM per node with a single A100‑backed GPU (or equivalent). Start with 4 nodes; add autoscaling up to 12 under sustained 5m load. We recommend using local NVMe for the KV cache with a 2x replication across the inference pool for resilience.
- Archive nodepool: we recommend giving each archival node 24 x 8TB NVMe drives in a JBOD configuration behind a wear‑aware layer; backing store should offer object semantics for easy export to your nearline tier. Use node affinity to avoid multi‑tenant cohabitation of archival disks.
- PVC tuning: set reclaimPolicy=Retain for snapshot PVs, and enforce a TTL controller that labels PVs for movement rather than instant deletion. That keeps an auditable trail for compliance.

I added a short checklist in the attached runbook page 2 for rack/network prep (public/private peering, SNAT pools, BGP peering if you plan cross‑region pulls). If you want, we can run a one‑hour sizing workshop with your infra folks next week and produce a capped BOM.

—Laura
